title: Esme's Super Roof
markdown:
The evening breeze whispered through the meadow, clover-sweet, lavender and rose in the sky. Esme, who loved to watch the stars, sat with Tumble, a woolly goat. Beside them Mrs. Quinn painted a birdhouse a gentle blue.

“A cozy home for our little friends,” Mrs. Quinn hummed. “But the roof must stay strong and dry if a big storm comes. We must keep their house snug.”

Esme’s eyes sparkled. “We must test it. To make the very best roof!”

Tumble’s ears wiggled. “Test? For the birdies? Fun!”

They made a special roof. First Esme laid a soft blanket over the house. Mrs. Quinn added pretend rain. The blanket soaked and dripped.

“Oh dear,” Tumble mumbled. “Not good for warm beds.”

Next, golden leaves piled around the roof. Water dripped through the little gaps.

“Lovely for a soft floor,” Mrs. Quinn said gently, “but perhaps not for a dry roof.”

Esme found a smooth flat pebble. “Water rolls right off!” Stiff cardboard: some water seeped, making it damp. “Strong, but maybe not totally dry.”

Tumble found a wide shiny plastic leaf. Water trickled, pooled, rolled off. The plastic stayed dry.

“Wow,” Esme breathed. “That water slides away so easily!”

Mrs. Quinn brought thin flexible wood, strong and smooth. Water sat on top, round and shiny, not soaking in at once — a kind of shield, if the slope helped.

Esme clapped softly. “The blanket and leaves soak or leak. The cardboard is strong but lets water through. The plastic leaf lets water roll off — waterproof. The thin wood is strong and helps keep water out. Plastic leaf and thin wood together. Best, driest roof!”

They cut the thin wood for the birdhouse, laid the shiny plastic over it, sloping just right. Honey-smelling glue. Water would have a way to leave.

Mrs. Quinn poured pretend rain. Not a drop inside. Plastic shone, water tumbled away, wood did not soak through.

“Different materials for different jobs,” Mrs. Quinn said, soft and warm. “The plastic pushes water away. The wood holds the shape. Together: the driest roof.”

Esme gazed at the little house. A wonderful puzzle, solved before the stars took over. Tumble nudged her hand with his soft head. Crickets. Snug paint still drying blue. They did not need a sermon on sleep. The roof would do the staying-dry; Esme and Tumble could do the watching-stars, until even that went gentle and quiet.
